abstract:
Persiathiacin A is a novel thiopeptide antibiotic produced
by Actinokineospora species UTMC 2448. It has potent
activity
against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis . Thiopeptides,
including persiathiacin A, exhibit antibacterial activity by inhibiting
protein synthesis. In this study, we characterize the mechanism of
action of persiathiacin A and investigate how resistance to this antibiotic
can emerge. In vitro assays revealed that persiathiacin
A inhibits translation elongation, leading to ribosome stalling. Genetic
analysis of resistant Bacillus subtilis mutants identified
mutations primarily in the rplK gene encoding ribosomal
protein L11, which is the binding site for other 26-membered macrocycle-containing
thiopeptides. The resistant mutants showed growth impairment and an
increased lag time, even in the absence of persiathiacin. Comparative
proteomic analysis of a resistant mutant versus the parental strain
revealed multiple changes, indicative of negative effects on protein
synthesis. Thus, although persiathiacin-resistant mutants can arise
readily by the loss of L11 function, it is likely that such mutants
would be severely compromised in pathogenesis. Furthermore, bioinformatics
analysis identified differences in the key amino acids within the
thiopeptide-binding region of L11 in the persiathiacin producer. These
probably prevent the antibiotic from associating with its target,
providing a mechanism for self-resistance.

General Experimental Procedure
An Agilent 1260 Infinity
II preparative HPLC connected to a semipreparative reverse-phase C18
Betasil column (21.2 × 150 mm) was used for purification of persiathiacin
A. LC-HR-MS analysis of the crude extract and pure fractions was performed
on a Thermo Vanquish UHPLC connected to a Proshell 120 EC-C18 column
(2.1 × 100 mm, 1.9 μm) linked to an Orbitrap IQ-X Tribrid
mass spectrometer. Proteomics analysis was performed on a ZenoTOF
7600 using a Poroshell 120 EC-C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.9 μm).
NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker 600 MHz spectrometer equipped
with a TCI cryoprobe at 25 °C. The
1
H and
13
C NMR chemical shifts were referenced to the DMSO-
d
6
solvent peaks at δ
H
2.50 and δ
C
39.52. All HPLC and
LC-MS experiments were performed with a MeCN-H
2
O gradient
solvent system.
Purification of Persiathiacin A
Actinokineospora
strain UTMC 2448 was grown on 1 L of YEME solid agar (10 g/L glucose,
5 g/L peptone, 3 g/L malt extract, 3 g/L yeast extract) for 7 days
at 30 °C. Agar plates were chopped into small pieces and extracted
with EtoAc for 3 h then dried on a rotary evaporator. Dried extract
was resuspended in 1 mL methanol, loaded onto dental cotton and air-dried
in a fume hood. The dental cotton containing the extract was loaded
into a cartridge (10 × 30 mm) connected to a semipreparative
reverse-phase C18 Betasil column (21.2 mm × 150 mm) connected
to an Agilent 1260 Infinity II preparative HPLC. The following method
was used for purification: initially, constant 5% acetonitrile for
5 min, followed by a linear gradient from 5 to 95% acetonitrile for
55 min, then isocratic at 100% acetonitrile for the next 5 min at
a flow rate of 9 min/mL. The fraction collector was set to collect
fractions at 60 s intervals throughout a 60 min runtime. Persiathiacin
A was eluted in fractions 38–39.
Ribosome Inhibition Assay
The ability of persiathiacin
A to inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis was assessed in an
E. coli
cell-free transcription/translation assay in which
production of firefly luciferase was monitored in the presence of
increasing concentrations of persiathiacin A. The assay was carried
out in triplicate as previously described.
36
IC
50
values were determined by least-squares regression
analysis as implemented in the GraphPad Prism software package.
In Vitro
Translation Assay
70S his-tagged
ribosomes (JE28), translation factors IF1–3, EF-Tu, EF-Ts and
EF-G, tRNAs and RelE were purified, and the mRNA used was transcribed,
PAGE purified and radiolabeled as described previously.
37
Aminoacylation (and formylation for fMet-tRNA)
of tRNAs were also completed as described.
37
Translation was initiated using 1 pmol radiolabeled mRNA, 120 pmol
70S ribosomes, 35 pmol each IF1–3, 200 pmol fMet-tRNA
fMet
, 4 mM GTP in 20 μL 1X coupling buffer (CB; 25 mM Tris-HCl
pH 7.4, 60 mM NH
4
Cl, 10 mM Mg(OAc)
2
, 6 mM β-Mercaptoethanol)
for eight min at 37 °C. Persiathiacin A was added at a concentration
of 0, 180, or 1300 μg/μL. Ribosomes were immobilized by
the addition of 5 μL High Performance Nickel-Sepharose beads
(Cytiva) and left shaking at RT for 5 min. The beads were washed twice
with CB and resuspended in sufficient CB, alongside imidazole to elute
ribosomes from the beads. Aliquots of 5 μL were added to each
elongation reaction.
During elongation, persiathiacin A was
added at concentrations between 0.312 and 1300 μg/μL,
or excluded. The overall reactions included 5 μL of initiated
ribosomes, 4 mM GTP, 2.5 μL of required persiathiacin/buffer,
500 pmol EF-Tu and EF-Ts, 1 nmol EF-G, 30 pmol each aa-tRNA
aa
(Phe, Val, Arg, Asp) in 25 μL CB, and incubated for 4 min
at 37 °C. Following the reaction, 5 μL samples were removed
and added to 5 μL of stop buffer (formamide and EDTA), while
another 5 μL sample was challenged with 1 μL RelE freezer
stock, for ten min at 37 °C, followed by addition of 5 μL
stop buffer. Each final reaction was heated to 95 °C for ten
min, then 1.5 μL of each reaction was loaded onto, and the products
were resolved, by 10% denaturing PAGE (8 M urea). Gels were dried
and exposed to phosphorimage plates overnight (Cytiva) and scanned
on a Typhoon (Cytiva), followed by analysis using ImageQuant (Cytiva).
Generation of
B. Subtilis
Resistant Mutants
All resistant mutants were derived from
B. subtilis
168CA. The overnight bacterial culture was refreshed in LB and grown
at 30 °C, and 160 rpm in a reciprocal shaking incubator to OD
600
nm of ∼0.4. Subsequently, 50 μL of refreshed
B. subtilis
168CA was spread onto nutrient agar plates containing
persiathiacin A at concentrations of 10 μg/mL, and incubated
at 30 °C. The resulting colonies were patched onto a nutrient
agar plate containing 10 μg/mL of persiathiacin A to confirm
they are resistant and then grown in LB liquid medium supplemented
with 10 μg/mL persiathiacin A for sequencing and glycerol stock
for −80 °C preservation.
B. Subtilis
Transformation
The
rplK
deletion mutant BKE01020 (
ΔrplK::erm
trpC2)
38
was obtained from the Bacillus
Genetic Stock Center. To transfer the mutation into the
B.
subtilis
168CA background, 4 mL of pretransformation medium
(
Table S2
) was heavily inoculated with
the parent strain. This was incubated at 37 °C with reciprocal
shaking until the OD
600
nm reached 3.5. Then 150 μL
of competent cells were added to 1 mL of prewarmed transformation
medium (
Table S2
) with either 50 μL
sterile water (no DNA control) or 50 μL genomic DNA, then incubated
at 37 °C with reciprocal shaking. Finally, 150 and 50 μL
volumes of the transformations were plated on selective medium containing
erythromycin (1 μg/mL) and incubated at 37 °C overnight.
Spot Test Analysis
First, 4 mL volumes of LB were inoculated
with target strains and incubated for 3–4 h at 37 °C with
reciprocal shaking. Then the OD
600
nm of these cultures
was measured and cultures were diluted to an OD
600
nm of
0.05, then incubated at 37 °C with shaking until the OD
600
nm reached 0.8. 10-fold dilutions of the cultures were carried out
using a 96-well plate. Finally, 5 μL of each of the dilution
series was plated on nutrient agar with or without persiathiacin.
Plates were incubated overnight at 37 °C prior to imaging.
MIC Growth Curve Analysis
Strains were inoculated into
1 mL of nutrient broth and incubated at 37 °C with reciprocal
shaking overnight. The overnight cultures were diluted 100-fold into
1 mL of fresh nutrient broth. Nutrient broth (135 μL) with
or without persiathiacin was added to the wells of a 96-well plate.
Then 15 μL aliquots of the diluted culture were seeded into
each well. A breath-easy film plate cover was applied before incubating
the plate in a TECAN plate reader for OD
600
nm measurement
at 6 min intervals. Results were exported into excel, and 0.12 was
subtracted from all readings to account for the background signal
from the medium. Time was plotted against log
10
(OD
600
nm) using GraphPad PRISM.
Whole Genome Sequencing Analysis
The genomes of the
parent strain
B. subtilis
168CA and 15 persiathiacin
A-resistant mutants were sequenced with Illumina short read sequencing
by MicrobesNG. Analysis of the sequencing data was executed by a CLC
genomics workbench (
https://digitalinsights.qiagen.com/products-overview/discovery-insights-portfolio/analysis-and-visualization/qiagen-clc-genomics-workbench/
). Raw sequence reads were aligned to a
B. subtilis
168CA reference genome (
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/AL009126.3/
). Then, to find common variants among the persiathiacin resistant
mutants, a basic variant search was performed on the aligned reads
prior to the exclusion of variants present in the parent strain.
Total Proteome Profiling
A preculture was prepared
by refreshing an overnight culture in LB (40 μL in 4 mL). At
an OD
600
nm between 0.2 and 0.5, 250 μL (wild type)
or 500 μL (mutant) of preculture was added to 25 mL of LB. At
OD
600
nm around 0.5, 20 mL of cell culture was centrifuged,
the supernatant discarded, and the cell pellet resuspended in 20 mL
PBS buffer. The cells were pelleted and concentrated by resuspension
in 800 μL of PBS, then divided into 200 μL aliquots in
4 Eppendorf tubes. One aliquot of cells was lysed with 250 μL
BugBuster master mix (Millipore) with 1.25 μL of lysozyme (final
concentration 50 μg/mL) and 2.5 μL of protease and phosphatase
inhibitor master mix was added and incubated at room temperature for
10–15 min. The mixture was centrifuged at 16,000
g
for 20 min at 4 °C to remove insoluble debris. Proteins were
precipitated using a chloroform/methanol method,
39
and solubilized in 6 M urea/2 M thiourea in 50 mM triethylammonium
bicarbonate (TEAB), pH 8.0. Proteins were reduced for 1 h with 10
mM DTT, and then alkylated for 30 min in the dark with 25 mM iodoacetamide
(IAA). Treated proteins were diluted with 0.6 M urea/0.2 M thiourea,
quantified using a Qubit (Thermo Scientific), and digested with MS-grade
porcine trypsin (1:50; Promega) for 18 h at 37 °C, followed by
clean up on an Oasis HLB cartridge (Waters). The cartridge was first
activated by 1 mL of methanol and 1 mL of acetonitrile and then washed
with 1 mL of water containing 0.1% TFA. Digested sample was passed
through the cartridge. After washing with 6 mL of water containing
0.1% TFA, peptides were eluted with 1.2 mL of 50% acetonitrile/water
(0.1% TFA).
Eluted peptides solution was dried on Genevac and
resuspended on 10 μL of water (0.1% FA) for analysis by liquid
chromatography, sequential window acquisition of all theoretical mass
spectra (LC-SWATH-MS). Peptides were separated using a Nexera Series
UHPLC LC-40 system (Shizmadzu, Kyoto, Japan) coupled to a Poroshell
120 EC-C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.9 μm) with a UHPLC guard
attached (Agilent). LC mobile phase consisted of A, water (0.1% formic
acid) B, acetonitrile (0.1% formic acid). The peptides were separated
using an initial linear gradient of 9 to 29% B over 5.6 min, then
29 to 42% B over 0.6 min, then 42 to 80% B over 0.2 min. The column
was washed with 80% B for 0.2 min before re-equilibrating with 3%
B. The flow rate was either 0.8 mL/min at peptide elution or 1 mL/min
at wash and equilibration, and the column was heated at 40 °C.
The separated peptides were analyzed with a ZenoToF 7600 (Sciex)
with the SWATH-MS experiment conducted in positive polarity. Ion source
gases were as follows; ion source 1:60 psi, ion source 2:65 psi, curtain
gas: 40 psi, and collision gas: 7 psi. Spray voltage was set to 4500
V and the heated capillary set to 700 °C. Ions were generated
by electrospray and data acquired in SWATH acquisition mode using
varying isolation widths of approximately 5–42
m
/
z
(containing 1
m
/
z
for the window overlap and decreasing in width toward 650
m
/
z
). A set of 60 overlapping windows was
constructed covering the precursor mass range of 400–900
m
/
z
and the effective isolation windows
can be considered as being 399.5–441.2, 440.2–459.9,
etc. SWATH MS2 spectra were collected from 100–1800
m
/
z
. The collision energy for each window
varied 19–43 V, starting at 19 V and increasing 1–2
V per window with increasing
m

z

in high-sensitivity mode, resulting in a total duty cycle of ∼0.627
s. Zeno pulsing was applied. The LC-MS output data were analyzed by
Spectronaut (Biognosys).

body:
The urgent global health concern
of antibiotic resistance highlights the crucial need for novel antibiotics,
especially against drug-resistant pathogens. Natural products, vital
since the inception of the antibiotic era in the mid-20th century,
remain potent therapeutic agents against pathogenic bacteria.
1
,
2
Thiopeptides, characterized by their intricate thiazole-containing
macrocyclic structures, are peptide-derived antibiotics of ribosomal
origin. They are part of a broader group of natural products termed
ribosomally biosynthesized and post-translationally modified peptides
(RiPPs).
3
Despite their structural diversity,
almost all known thiopeptide antibiotics act as inhibitors of protein
synthesis. Their exact mode of action varies depending on the number
and type of residues within the central macrocycle.
4
Thiostrepton, thiocillin (micrococcin), and nosiheptide,
which are characterized by their 26-membered primary macrocycles,
operate by binding to the interface of ribosomal protein L11 and the
23S rRNA (specifically, helix 43 and 44) within the bacterial 50S
ribosomal subunit (
Figure
1
).
5
−
9
This binding site, widely conserved throughout evolution, is referred
to as the guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase)-associated center (GAC).
10
Importantly, this site differs from those targeted
by clinically utilized antibiotics,
11
which
contributes to the ability of thiopeptides to overcome existing drug
resistance.
Figure 1
A) Structure of the 26-membered thiopeptides persiathiacin A, nosiheptide,
thiocillin I, and thiostrepton. B) X-ray structure of thiostrepton
(left) and nosiheptide (right) bound at the interface of 23S rRNA
(gold) and L11 (cyan) of the 50S ribosomal subunit of
Deinococcus
radiodurans
. Structures were obtained from Protein Data Bank
(accession numbers:
3CF5
(thiostrepton) and
2ZJP
(nosiheptide)).
In the process of translation, GAC interacts with
elongation factors
G (EF-G) and 4 (EF4), stimulating their GTPase activities, which are
essential for the translocation of ribosome-associated mRNA and tRNA
molecules, including the peptidyl-tRNA carrying the nascent peptide
chain. For thiostrepton and nosiheptide, their binding obstructs the
GAC, thus impeding the productive interactions of EF-G and EF4 with
the ribosome and ultimately inhibiting protein synthesis.
12
−
14
Additionally, it has been shown that thiostrepton can hinder translation
initiation because initiation factor 2 (IF-2) binds to the same site
during assembly of the 70S ribosome.
15
,
16
Despite
the potent antibacterial activity of thiopeptides, their
development into clinically useful antibiotics has been limited by
their low aqueous solubility. As a result, their use has been restricted
to thiostrepton and nosiheptide as topical ointments and in animal
feed. Persiathiacin A is a novel 26-membered polyglycosylated thiopeptide
produced by
Actinokineospora
strain UTMC 2448 (
Figure
1
). It has potent
activity against MRSA (MIC of 0.025 μg/mL) and drug-resistant
clinical isolates of
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
(MICs
of 1.6–3.7 μg/mL).
17
The MIC
value obtained for persiathiacin A against MRSA is close to the range
that has been reported for nosiheptide against various MRSA strains
(0.03–0.125 μg/mL),
18
which
suggests that polyglycosylation has little impact on activity. The
discovery and biosynthetic elucidation of persiathiacin A, has provided
a valuable foundation for biosynthetic engineering to create new glycosylated
thiopeptide derivatives with improved aqueous solubility and enhanced
therapeutic potential.
17
Herein we present
biochemical and genetic studies unveiling both the mechanism of action
and the mechanisms of resistance to persiathiacin A.
Results and Discussion
Inhibition of Translation Elongation
in Vitro
by Persiathiacin A
Based on previous work investigating
the mode of action of related thiopeptide antibiotics, we investigated
the ability of persiathiacin A to inhibit protein synthesis using
an
in vitro
coupled transcription-translation assay.
Persiathiacin A inhibits the synthesis of a luciferase reporter read
out in a dose-dependent manner with an IC
50
of 1.8 ±
0.3 μM (
Figure
2
). To understand in more detail how persiathiacin A blocks protein
synthesis, including the stage of translation targeted, we utilized
an
in vitro
translation system, built from purified
E. coli
components, to challenge ribosomes with the antibiotic
in both translation initiation and translation elongation. These reactions
begin with 70S ribosome assembly on a 5′-radiolabeled bespoke
mRNA, containing a ribosome binding site and a short coding region
from an initiation codon through to a stop codon (
Figure
3
a), using translation initiation
factors 1, 2 and 3, alongside the initiator tRNA, fMet-tRNA
fMet
. Following initiation, ribosomes within the initiation complex are
immobilized on Ni-NTA-Sepharose beads via a His
6
tag on
ribosomal protein L12,
19
allowing washing
to remove and swap components. Initiation complexes are then eluted
from the beads using imidazole to allow the addition of elongation
factors. During elongation, aminoacyl tRNA substrates in ternary complexes
with EF-Tu/GTP are provided to the ribosome alongside EF-G/GTP, which
eventually leads the ribosome to the stop codon. The ribosome’s
position on the mRNA at any stage can be determined through addition
of the ribosome-dependent endonuclease RelE, which cleaves mRNA specifically
within the A-site of the ribosome. The effect of persiathiacin A was
investigated by addition at either the initiation or elongation steps.
Figure 2
Concentration-dependent
inhibition of
E. coli
ribosomes
by persiathiacin A.
Figure 3
In vitro
translation to investigate the
effect
of persiathiacin A on translation initiation and elongation. A)
In vitro
translation mRNA schematic. The coding region on
the right-hand side is annotated with single letter amino acids names.
B) Denaturing PAGE loaded with radiolabeled RNA products following
the persiathiacin challenge during translation initiation and elongation.
RelE was added post elongation. C) Denaturing PAGE loaded with radiolabeled
RNA products following persiathiacin challenge during translation
elongation.
When added during initiation, persiathiacin A did
not prevent translation
initiation complex assembly on the mRNA, as can be seen from the RelE
cleavage of mRNA at the codon positioned in the vacant A-site of the
initiated ribosome (F codon;
Figure
3
B, compare lanes 2, 10, and 18). In the absence of
the antibiotic, ribosomes translated to the end of the coding sequence,
as confirmed by the RelE cleavage at the stop codon (
Figure
3
B, lane 24 and
Figure
3
C lane 12). However, addition
of the antibiotic during either initiation or elongation prevented
translation elongation. When added during elongation, ribosomes tended
to stall, especially at the first two codons immediately after the
start codon (
Figure
3
B, lanes 4, 6, 12, 14, and 22). Translation elongation was inhibited
at all concentrations tested from 1250 μg/μL down to 312
ng/μL (
Figure
3
C, lanes 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 16, and 18). The apparent reduction of
inhibition at 1300 μg/μL of the antibiotic (
Figure
3
B, lane 20, and partially notable
in lanes 4 and 12) is explained by precipitation at high concentrations
upon addition to the aqueous reaction mixture. Interestingly, when
the ribosome was challenged with persiathiacin A during initiation,
even after multiple washings of immobilized initiation complexes,
the ribosomes failed to proceed through to elongation, suggesting
some kind of “persistent poisoning” effect (
Figure
3
B, lanes 8 and 16).
One possible explanation for this would be that the dehydroalanine
moiety in persiathiacin acts as a Michael acceptor and irreversibly
binds to a ribosomal component, thereby affecting translation.
The mechanism by which thiopeptides are taken up, allowing them
to enter the cytoplasm and interact with the ribosome in Gram-positive
bacteria, remains an intriguing, yet unresolved question. Thiopeptides
are generally ineffective against Gram-negative bacteria, likely due
to the outer membrane’s impermeability to these large, hydrophobic
compounds. However, thiostrepton and thiocillin have been shown to
inhibit the growth of
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
under
iron-limiting conditions. In these cases, uptake occurs through the
siderophore pyoverdine receptors FpvA and FpvB (for thiostrepton)
and the ferrioxamine receptor FoxA (for thiocillin).
20
,
21
These studies have demonstrated that the mechanism of action for
thiostrepton and thiocillin in
P. aeruginosa
is similar
to that in Gram-positive bacteria, involving inhibition of protein
synthesis.
20
,
21
Mechanisms of Resistance to Persiathiacin A
To decipher
the mechanisms behind the development of resistance to persiathiacin
A, we selected resistant mutants in
B. subtilis
168CA
using nutrient agar (NA) plates containing 10 μg/mL of the antibiotic.
After 48 h of incubation, colonies of resistant mutants emerged. To
elucidate the genetic basis of this resistance, we sequenced the genomes
of 15 independent resistant isolates along with the parent,
B. subtilis
168CA, using short-read Illumina technology.
Comparative analysis revealed the presence of base substitutions in
or just upstream of the
rplK
gene, encoding ribosomal
protein L11, in all resistant mutants (
Table S1
). Half of the mutants exhibited a CAC deletion spanning bases 62–64
of
rplK
, resulting in deletion of the Pro22 residue
in ribosomal protein L11 (
Figure S1
). Pro22
is located on the surface of ribosomal protein L11 bound by thiostrepton
and nosiheptide (corresponding to Pro21 of L11 from
D. radiodurans
, shown in
Figure
1
; see also
Figure S2
).
6
,
8
,
13
The remaining
rplK
mutants
displayed either deletions causing frameshifts or point mutations
affecting the initiation codon, presumably again resulting in a loss
of L11 function. Additional sequence lesions were found upstream of
either the 16S or 5S rRNA genes in all except two of the mutants.
It seems possible that these are secondary mutations, selected as
a result of the deleterious growth consequences arising from loss
of L11 (see below). To determine whether the resistance mechanism
in
S. aureus
also involves the loss of L11 function,
resistant mutants were selected using the same approach employed for
selecting
B. subtilis
mutants. The
rplK
gene from the 6 independent mutants and the parental strain was
PCR amplified and sequenced. Multiple sequence alignments revealed
point mutations in the
rplK
gene, causing frameshifts
or early stop codons that led to a truncated L11 protein. Additionally,
in two resistant isolates, 57 nucleotides (positions 87 to 143) were
deleted in
rplK
(
Figure S3
). Since we only sequenced the
rplK
region of a
few
S. aureus
mutant isolates, we cannot rule out
the possibility that
S. aureus
may have additional
resistance mechanisms to persiathiacin A beyond the L11 mutations
described.
Given that all mutants featured mutations affecting
ribosomal protein L11, and considering previous evidence implicating
rplK
deletions in
B. subtilis
thiostrepton
resistance,
22
we investigated whether loss
of ribosomal protein L11 alone confers resistance to persiathiacin.
The effect of different concentrations of persiathiacin A on growth
of wild type
B. subtilis
168CA, a representative
selected mutant (MutD) and a
rplK
deletion strain,
was tested (
Figure
4
). Growth of the wild type strain was partially inhibited at concentrations
of 0.01 or 0.02 μg/mL persiathiacin A (
Figure
4
A). In contrast, the MutD and
ΔrplK
strains were completely resistant to persiathiacin A up to the highest
concentration tested (45 μg/mL;
Figure
4
A). It was also noticeable that both mutant
strains had an extended lag phase (about 6–7 h compared to
3 h for wild type), and significantly slower growth rates than the
wild type (doubling times of about 3.5 and 1.2 h, respectively). Dilutions
of cultures of the three strains were then tested for growth on plates
containing zero or 15 μg/mL persiathiacin A (
Figure
4
B). Again, the two mutant strains,
but not the wild type, exhibited resistance to the antibiotic, though
again they appeared to grow more slowly in its absence (
Figure
4
B).
Figure 4
Effects of persiathiacin
A on mutant and wild type
B. subtilis
strains. A)
Growth of strains:
B. subtilis
168CA
(left),
B. subtilis
168CA MutD (middle), and
B. subtilis ΔrplK
(BKE01020) (right), in NB medium
containing the indicated concentrations of persiathiacin A. B) Cultures
of the indicated strains were serially diluted, and 5 μL samples
were spotted on NA plates with (left) and without (right) 15 μg/μL
persiathiacin.
It was curious that mutation of the
rplK
gene
conferred a high level resistance to pesiathiacin A but also impaired
growth. As one way to investigate this, we conducted a comparative
proteomics analysis between one of the mutants (MutD) and the parental
strain
B. subtilis
168CA. Indeed, as expected, mutation
in ribosomal protein L11 led to increased proteome stress as judged
by the nature of several of the proteins whose levels were altered
(
Figure
5
). For example,
both small and large chaperonin subunits GroES and GroEL, which collectively
form a nanocage facilitating proper folding of newly translated or
translocated proteins, were upregulated.
23
,
24
Conversely, translation initiation factor 2 (IF-2) (InfB), which
interacts with the GAC,
25
was found to
be downregulated in the mutant strain, as was the ribosome hibernation
promotion factor (HPF) (Hst23), crucial for ribosome dimerization
in stationary phase and the protection of essential ribosomal proteins.
26
,
27
Figure 5
Volcano
plot of the comparative proteomics analysis between
B. subtilis
168CA MutD and its parental strain
B.
subtilis
168CA. The cutoff values, q = 0.05 and fold change
= 2, are indicated by dashed lines.
The levels of many other proteins not obviously
directly associated
with protein synthesis were also significantly altered. Some of the
more highly upregulated proteins included YcdA, a lipoprotein involved
in swarming motility,
28
YukE, a WXG100
virulence factor homologue, and YukC, responsible for the export of
YukE.
29
The function of the most up-regulated
protein YoyC remains unknown. Among the downregulated proteins, notable
enzymes involved in cysteine uptake, biosynthesis, and metabolism
were identified. These include
l
-cysteine uptake protein
TcyP,
30
SAT (Sulfate adenylyltransferase),

Self-resistance in the thiostrepton

Conclusions
This study provides strong evidence that
the unusual polyglycoslated
thiopeptide antibiotic persiathiacin A kills bacteria by directly
inhibiting protein synthesis and reveals how bacteria can develop
resistance to persiathiacin A. The genetic basis for resistance was
identified as mutations within the
rplK
gene, encoding
ribosomal protein L11, which plays a crucial role in the binding of
other 26-membered macrocycle-containing thiopeptides. This was consistent
with biochemical studies showing that persiathiacin A stalls ribosomal
protein elongation. These results illustrate that despite the polyglycosylation
of the core peptide, the target remains unchanged. Binding of other
thiopeptides to ribosomal protein L11 disrupts conformational transitions
of EF-G and EF4 stabilized by interactions with the 23S rRNA/ribosomal
protein L11 complex, leading to stalling of translation during the
elongation step of bacterial protein synthesis. Curiously initiation
of translation was not affected by the antibiotic, even though IF-2
binds at GAC, suggesting that persiathiacin A may have a subtly different
mechanism of action than thiostrepton. The resistant mutants displayed
altered growth characteristics and distinct proteomic profiles, with
significant changes in the expression of proteins related to protein
folding, motility, and ribosome protection. The reduced growth rates
of the resistant mutants could be advantageous for antibiotic therapy
by rendering the strains less fit than the wild type. Bioinformatics
analyses suggest that self-resistance in the persiathiacin producer
is due to multiple alterations to the thiopeptide-binding region of
L11, preventing association of the antibiotic with its target.
Methods
General Experimental Procedure
An Agilent 1260 Infinity
II preparative HPLC connected to a semipreparative reverse-phase C18
Betasil column (21.2 × 150 mm) was used for purification of persiathiacin
A. LC-HR-MS analysis of the crude extract and pure fractions was performed
on a Thermo Vanquish UHPLC connected to a Proshell 120 EC-C18 column
(2.1 × 100 mm, 1.9 μm) linked to an Orbitrap IQ-X Tribrid
mass spectrometer. Proteomics analysis was performed on a ZenoTOF
7600 using a Poroshell 120 EC-C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.9 μm).
NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker 600 MHz spectrometer equipped
with a TCI cryoprobe at 25 °C. The
1
H and
13
C NMR chemical shifts were referenced to the DMSO-
d
6
solvent peaks at δ
H
2.50 and δ
C
39.52. All HPLC and
LC-MS experiments were performed with a MeCN-H
2
O gradient
solvent system.
Purification of Persiathiacin A
Actinokineospora
strain UTMC 2448 was grown on 1 L of YEME solid agar (10 g/L glucose,
5 g/L peptone, 3 g/L malt extract, 3 g/L yeast extract) for 7 days
at 30 °C. Agar plates were chopped into small pieces and extracted
with EtoAc for 3 h then dried on a rotary evaporator. Dried extract
was resuspended in 1 mL methanol, loaded onto dental cotton and air-dried
in a fume hood. The dental cotton containing the extract was loaded
into a cartridge (10 × 30 mm) connected to a semipreparative
reverse-phase C18 Betasil column (21.2 mm × 150 mm) connected
to an Agilent 1260 Infinity II preparative HPLC. The following method
was used for purification: initially, constant 5% acetonitrile for
5 min, followed by a linear gradient from 5 to 95% acetonitrile for
55 min, then isocratic at 100% acetonitrile for the next 5 min at
a flow rate of 9 min/mL. The fraction collector was set to collect
fractions at 60 s intervals throughout a 60 min runtime. Persiathiacin
A was eluted in fractions 38–39.
Ribosome Inhibition Assay
The ability of persiathiacin
A to inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis was assessed in an
E. coli
cell-free transcription/translation assay in which
production of firefly luciferase was monitored in the presence of
increasing concentrations of persiathiacin A. The assay was carried
out in triplicate as previously described.
36
IC
50
values were determined by least-squares regression
analysis as implemented in the GraphPad Prism software package.

Translation Assay
70S his-tagged
ribosomes (JE28), translation factors IF1–3, EF-Tu, EF-Ts and
EF-G, tRNAs and RelE were purified, and the mRNA used was transcribed,
PAGE purified and radiolabeled as described previously.
37
Aminoacylation (and formylation for fMet-tRNA)
of tRNAs were also completed as described.
37
Translation was initiated using 1 pmol radiolabeled mRNA, 120 pmol
70S ribosomes, 35 pmol each IF1–3, 200 pmol fMet-tRNA
fMet
, 4 mM GTP in 20 μL 1X coupling buffer (CB; 25 mM Tris-HCl
pH 7.4, 60 mM NH
4
Cl, 10 mM Mg(OAc)
2
, 6 mM β-Mercaptoethanol)
for eight min at 37 °C. Persiathiacin A was added at a concentration
of 0, 180, or 1300 μg/μL. Ribosomes were immobilized by
the addition of 5 μL High Performance Nickel-Sepharose beads
(Cytiva) and left shaking at RT for 5 min. The beads were washed twice
with CB and resuspended in sufficient CB, alongside imidazole to elute
ribosomes from the beads. Aliquots of 5 μL were added to each

During elongation, persiathiacin A was
added at concentrations between 0.312 and 1300 μg/μL,
or excluded. The overall reactions included 5 μL of initiated

All resistant mutants were derived from

Total Proteome Profiling
A preculture was prepared
by refreshing an overnight culture in LB (40 μL in 4 mL). At
an OD
600
nm between 0.2 and 0.5, 250 μL (wild type)
or 500 μL (mutant) of preculture was added to 25 mL of LB. At
OD
600
nm around 0.5, 20 mL of cell culture was centrifuged,
the supernatant discarded, and the cell pellet resuspended in 20 mL
PBS buffer. The cells were pelleted and concentrated by resuspension
in 800 μL of PBS, then divided into 200 μL aliquots in
4 Eppendorf tubes. One aliquot of cells was lysed with 250 μL
BugBuster master mix (Millipore) with 1.25 μL of lysozyme (final
concentration 50 μg/mL) and 2.5 μL of protease and phosphatase
inhibitor master mix was added and incubated at room temperature for
10–15 min. The mixture was centrifuged at 16,000
g
for 20 min at 4 °C to remove insoluble debris. Proteins were
precipitated using a chloroform/methanol method,
39
and solubilized in 6 M urea/2 M thiourea in 50 mM triethylammonium
bicarbonate (TEAB), pH 8.0. Proteins were reduced for 1 h with 10
mM DTT, and then alkylated for 30 min in the dark with 25 mM iodoacetamide
(IAA). Treated proteins were diluted with 0.6 M urea/0.2 M thiourea,
quantified using a Qubit (Thermo Scientific), and digested with MS-grade
porcine trypsin (1:50; Promega) for 18 h at 37 °C, followed by
clean up on an Oasis HLB cartridge (Waters). The cartridge was first
activated by 1 mL of methanol and 1 mL of acetonitrile and then washed
with 1 mL of water containing 0.1% TFA. Digested sample was passed
through the cartridge. After washing with 6 mL of water containing
0.1% TFA, peptides were eluted with 1.2 mL of 50% acetonitrile/water
(0.1% TFA).
Eluted peptides solution was dried on Genevac and
resuspended on 10 μL of water (0.1% FA) for analysis by liquid
chromatography, sequential window acquisition of all theoretical mass
spectra (LC-SWATH-MS). Peptides were separated using a Nexera Series
UHPLC LC-40 system (Shizmadzu, Kyoto, Japan) coupled to a Poroshell
120 EC-C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.9 μm) with a UHPLC guard
attached (Agilent). LC mobile phase consisted of A, water (0.1% formic
acid) B, acetonitrile (0.1% formic acid). The peptides were separated
using an initial linear gradient of 9 to 29% B over 5.6 min, then
29 to 42% B over 0.6 min, then 42 to 80% B over 0.2 min. The column
was washed with 80% B for 0.2 min before re-equilibrating with 3%
B. The flow rate was either 0.8 mL/min at peptide elution or 1 mL/min
at wash and equilibration, and the column was heated at 40 °C.
The separated peptides were analyzed with a ZenoToF 7600 (Sciex)
with the SWATH-MS experiment conducted in positive polarity. Ion source
gases were as follows; ion source 1:60 psi, ion source 2:65 psi, curtain
gas: 40 psi, and collision gas: 7 psi. Spray voltage was set to 4500
V and the heated capillary set to 700 °C. Ions were generated
by electrospray and data acquired in SWATH acquisition mode using
varying isolation widths of approximately 5–42
m
/
z
(containing 1
m
/
z
for the window overlap and decreasing in width toward 650
m
/
z
). A set of 60 overlapping windows was
constructed covering the precursor mass range of 400–900
m
/
z
and the effective isolation windows
can be considered as being 399.5–441.2, 440.2–459.9,

/

. The collision energy for each window
